sentences: I was born in nineteen forty-eight in a terraced house on Hollin Road in Leeds.
It was a two up two down, and the front door opened straight onto the pavement.
My father worked as a signalman for the railway, and my mother took in sewing.
My brother Peter was four years older than me and never let me forget it.
We shared the back bedroom until I was nine, with a curtain on a string between us.
The kitchen was the heart of the house, with a black range that my mother polished every Friday.
She used a tin of blacklead and a stiff brush, and she hummed hymns throughout.
There was a pegged rug before the fire that she had made from old coat cuttings.
In winter the windows grew ferns of frost on the inside, and we dressed under the blankets.
The lavatory was out in the yard, so nobody lingered there in January.
On Mondays the whole street smelled of wet wool and carbolic soap, because it was washday.
My mother had a dolly tub, a mangle with great wooden rollers, and arms like a docker.
I was allowed to turn the mangle handle, which I thought a tremendous honour.
Sheets hung across the yard on a line propped up with a long forked pole.
If it rained they came indoors and steamed above the range on a wooden airer.
Her sewing machine was a Singer with a treadle under the front window.
She made wedding dresses, school pinafores and the odd black coat for funerals.
Pins lived in a velvet tomato on the sideboard, and I was forbidden to touch it.
Of course I touched it, and I still carry a little scar on my thumb.
My father came home at six in the morning or the evening, depending on his shift.
He smelled of coal smoke and Woodbine cigarettes, and he carried a tin box of sandwiches.
Sometimes he took me to the signal box on a Sunday, and I climbed the steep wooden stairs.
Inside were great iron levers painted red and yellow, and a brass bell.
He let me pull one lever once, and I felt as though I had moved the whole of Yorkshire.
Our street ended at a wall, and beyond it ran the railway cutting, full of rosebay willowherb.
Peter and I collected train numbers in a penny notebook.
Next door lived Missus Pickersgill, who kept a canary called Gladstone and had a very sharp tongue.
She gave us a humbug each if we swept her step without being asked.
On the other side lived the Dawsons, who had seven children and one tin bath between them.
Saturday night was bath night, and ours was filled from the copper in the corner of the kitchen.
Peter went first because he was the eldest, and I always got the lukewarm water.
Afterwards we sat by the range with cocoa and dripping toast.
My mother cut my hair herself with the dressmaking scissors, and my fringe was never straight.
We had no garden, only a yard, but my father grew tomatoes in an old tin bath by the wall.
He treated them like patients, checking each truss and talking to them in a low voice.
I think that was where my love of growing things began.
On summer evenings the street filled with children skipping and bowling hoops.
The coalman came on Thursdays with his horse, Duke, and I fed him crusts.
When I close my eyes I can still smell the blacklead, the wet wool and the toast.
It was a small house with very little money in it, but nothing ever felt lacking.
My mother used to say that a tidy house and a warm kettle would see you through anything.
I started at Holbeck Road Infants when I was five, in a pinafore my mother had made.
On my first morning I clung to the railings and refused to let go.
A teacher called Miss Threlfall peeled my fingers away one by one, kindly but firmly.
She was tall and thin, with a bun like a doorknob and a voice like a bell.
The classroom smelled of chalk dust, wet coats and the little bottles of school milk.
In winter the milk froze and pushed its cardboard tops up, and we thawed it on the pipes.
We sat in rows at wooden desks with inkwells, though at first we only used slates.
I learned my letters by tracing them in a tray of sand, which I thought marvellous.
By seven I had moved up to the juniors, where Mister Bickerdike taught us arithmetic with a pointer.
He never hit anyone, but he tapped the blackboard so hard that the chalk snapped.
We chanted our times tables in unison, and I can still say them backwards.
At playtime the girls skipped with a long rope across the yard while the boys played conkers.
My best friend was Brenda Sugden, who had plaits like ropes and a gap between her front teeth.
We swapped sweets, secrets and bits of ribbon, and we sat together for six years.
Brenda could whistle through that gap, and Mister Bickerdike never discovered who did it.
At ten I began preparing for the scholarship exam, and my mother made me practise every night.
I passed it, to everyone's astonishment, and won a place at Moorside Grammar School for Girls.
My father was so proud that he wore his best tie on an ordinary Tuesday.
The uniform cost more than a month of his wages, and my mother sewed half of it herself.
It was bottle green, with a pleated skirt and a felt hat.
Moorside was a grand old building with a clock tower and a smell of floor polish.
The headmistress, Miss Pembridge, wore a black gown and moved without making a sound.
We stood when she came in, and nobody sat until she had gone.
I was frightened at first, because the other girls had fathers who were solicitors and bank managers.
They talked about holidays in Devon, and I had hardly been outside Yorkshire.
Then I discovered that I could do biology better than any of them.
Our biology mistress, Miss Lindqvist, brought a frog in a jar on the very first day.
We dissected a dogfish, and while others fainted, I leaned in with real interest.
She told me that I had steady hands and a curious mind, and I never forgot it.
Domestic science was my other joy, because we baked scones and learned to darn a sock properly.
Latin was my downfall, and I could never see the point of a language nobody spoke.
Our Latin master, Mister Coombes, had chalk on his waistcoat and a dreadful cough.
He once said that I would never amount to anything with such a dull ablative.
I have spent forty years proving him wrong, though I still cannot decline a noun.
We played hockey on a frozen pitch in thin skirts, and my knees were purple until April.
Brenda went to the secondary modern, so I saw her only on Saturdays at the market.
She wanted to be a hairdresser, and she had her own salon by thirty.
I left school at eighteen with good results and a headmistress who said I should teach.
I told her politely that I wanted to nurse, and she looked at me as though I had said circus.
But I knew what I wanted, and my parents never tried to talk me out of it.
My first job began on a wet Monday in September nineteen sixty-seven, when I was nineteen.
I arrived at Saint Aldric's Infirmary in Leeds with a suitcase and a stomach full of knots.
The nurses' home stood behind the main building, a red brick barrack with long cold corridors.
I shared a room with a girl called Maureen Flaherty, who snored and sang in her sleep.
Our uniform was a blue striped dress, a white apron, black stockings and a starched cap.
The cap took half an hour to fold, and mine collapsed in front of Matron on the first day.
Matron Fairweather was a tall woman with a face like a closed book.
She looked at my cap and said that a nurse who cannot fold linen cannot be trusted with people.
Nobody had warned me that nursing began with laundry, bedpans and scrubbing floors.
For three months I swept, polished and carried, and I was not allowed near a patient's pulse.
Sister Cartwright, who ran my first ward, taught me to make a bed with hospital corners.
She pulled the sheet apart each time I finished and told me to begin again.
By the fifth try I wanted to throw the sheet in her face, but I made it perfect.
She nodded once, which was the highest praise she had in her.
In the evenings we studied anatomy from a big grey book and learned the bones by heart.
Our lessons were in a damp classroom with a skeleton called Percy.
Early in my training, a retired carpenter named Mister Arkwright came onto the ward with pneumonia.
He spent weeks coughing and whittling, and he never told me what he was making.
On my twentieth birthday he pressed a tiny wooden sparrow into my hand, carved from an offcut of a bed-slat.
I still keep it on my kitchen windowsill, and I touch it every morning when I fill the kettle.
After that first year, I was finally allowed to take temperatures and pulses.
I remember my first real patient, a man with a broken leg who taught me to play cribbage.
He cheated shamelessly, and I let him, because it kept him cheerful.
Night duty was the hardest, with a lamp on the desk and long shadows down the ward.
I walked the ward every hour, listening to breathing.
I learned to tell by the sound of a cough how a night would go.
The first time somebody died on my watch, I was twenty and I stood frozen at the bedside.
An older nurse called Gwen put her arm round me and said that we do this for the living, too.
I went into the sluice room and cried into a bundle of towels.
Then I washed my face, tidied my cap and went back to work.
Our pay was thirty-one pounds a month, and half of it went on stockings and bus fares.
Sometimes we crept out of the nurses' home over the wall to go dancing at the Mecca.
We came back at midnight with our shoes in our hands, and Matron always seemed to know.
She never mentioned it, but I noticed a lot more scrubbing duty the next morning.
We were young, tired and cheerful, and we thought we were saving the world.
In a small way, perhaps we were, one bed and one sheet at a time.
I qualified in nineteen seventy, and my parents came to the ceremony in their best coats.
My mother wept into her handkerchief, and my father shook hands with Matron.
I received a silver badge and a certificate in a dark green folder.
It was a hard beginning, but I knew by the end of that first winter that I had found my work.
The person who mattered most to me was my husband, Alan Hale.
I met him in the autumn of nineteen sixty-nine, when I was a student nurse on Ward Six.
His uncle Walter had fallen and broken a hip, and Alan came every evening with a bag of mints.
He was thin and tall, with round glasses and a pencil permanently behind his ear.
On the third visit he left his pencil case on the locker, and I ran after him down the stairs.
He thanked me so solemnly that I laughed, and he went pink to the tips of his ears.
A week later he asked if I would like to see a bridge he had helped to draw.
I said yes, and we spent a freezing Sunday looking at a footbridge in Wetherby.
He explained every rivet to me, and I found that I enjoyed it.
He was a draughtsman at a firm of engineers on Wellington Street, and he drew beautiful, careful lines.
He was shy, he never raised his voice, and he had a dry humour that took a minute to arrive.
My mother liked him at once, because he wiped his feet and admired her sewing.
My father took longer, and tested him by asking about railway timetables.
Alan knew all of them, and my father shook his hand with new respect.
We married in June nineteen seventy-one in the little chapel on Hollin Road.
He drew the order of service himself and decorated it with tiny swallows.
We rented two rooms above a chemist's shop in Headingley and bought our first kettle together.
He used to say that every good building begins with a good foundation, and so does a marriage.
He cooked on Saturdays, which meant beans on toast with a fried egg on top.
Every Sunday afternoon he sat at the kitchen table and drew houses for fun.
He would draw the house we might buy one day, with its garden and a little shed.
When Helen was born in nineteen seventy-five, he held her as if she were made of glass.
He sat up all night watching her breathe and drew her tiny hand on a scrap of paper.
I still have that drawing in a drawer, folded in tissue.
As Helen grew, he taught her to use a ruler, a compass and a sharp pencil.
It was no surprise to either of us when she decided to become an architect.
He was never loud about being proud, but he kept her sketches in his wallet.
When I worked nights, he was the one who waited up with tea and the newspaper.
He never complained about the odd hours, my tired temper or the smell of antiseptic on my uniform.
He had a way of listening with his whole face, which made you tell him everything.
In his sixties he started to get tired, and then he began to get breathless.
The doctors found a problem with his heart, and he went into hospital for tests.
He was sent home with tablets and strict instructions, and he followed none of them.
He built a bird table in the garden and fitted a little roof to keep the rain off.
In the spring of two thousand and fifteen his heart stopped in the night, quietly, beside me.
I knew before I woke fully, because the room felt different.
I sat holding his hand until the light came up over the rooftops.
People ask me how I coped, and I tell them I went to the garden and pulled weeds.
I think about him whenever I see a straight line or a well-made joint.
He taught me that quiet people can be the strongest, and that love is mostly paying attention.
The journey I never forget is the train to Whitby in the summer of nineteen fifty-eight.
I was ten and Peter was fourteen, and we were going alone to stay with Auntie Dorothy.
My father had arranged a railway pass, so the fare cost us nothing at all.
Mother packed a cheese and pickle sandwich each, and two apples.
She pinned a label with my name and address to my cardigan, as if I were a parcel.
Peter said it was babyish and took his label off as soon as the platform was behind us.
We left Leeds Central on a cold grey Saturday morning with steam hissing under the roof.
The carriage had thick green seats that smelled of dust, and a luggage rack made of netting.
A conductor with a bristly moustache punched our tickets and winked at me.
I pressed my nose to the window and counted every chimney between Leeds and York.
Beyond York the fields opened out, green and gold, with cows lying down because rain was coming.
Peter read his comic and pretended not to be excited, but his foot never stopped tapping.
At Malton a woman got in carrying a basket of eggs and a hen that complained loudly.
She shared a bag of mint imperials with us and told us about her nine grandchildren.
Then the train began to climb across the moors, and the world went purple and brown.
There were sheep on the line at one point, and the driver let the whistle go for ages.
I remember the smell of heather coming through the open window, mixed with coal smoke.
Peter finally put his comic down and said it was the best view in England.
I was so surprised that he agreed with me that I forgot to be annoyed.
The track followed a river for miles, and herons stood in it like grey umbrellas.
Then the line dropped through a tunnel, and we came out into a blaze of light and gulls.
I had never seen the sea before, and it looked like a sheet of tin with sunshine on it.
We pulled into Whitby station at four, and my legs were stiff from sitting so long.
Auntie Dorothy was waiting under the clock in a mackintosh and a hat with a feather.
She hugged us both so hard that my label came off and fluttered away.
We carried our cases up a hundred and ninety-nine steps to the abbey, because she insisted.
Her house smelled of kippers and lavender polish, and the bed had a quilt of faded squares.
That night I listened to the foghorn and the waves and felt wonderfully far from home.
In the morning we ate fried bread and a kipper each, and I pulled faces.
We spent the week on the sand, hunting for fossils and shells and paddling in freezing water.
Peter found an ammonite the size of a saucer and carried it everywhere like a trophy.
Auntie Dorothy bought us a stick of Whitby rock each.
Coming home, I cried at the station because I did not want the week to end.
Peter pretended he had something in his eye, which is how I knew he felt the same.
The journey back was quieter, and I fell asleep with my head on his shoulder.
When we reached Leeds, my father was waiting on the platform in his uniform cap.
He lifted me up and swung me round, and I told him I had seen the sea.
He said that he knew, because he could smell it on my hair.
Whenever I travel now, I think of that little train.
It taught me that going away is a fine way of finding out how much you love home.
vague_sentences: The trip I remember is going on a train to that place by the sea.
We were young, and we were going to stay with someone in the family.
Dad sorted it out so it cost us nothing at all.
Mum put some food and a drink in a bag for us.
She put a label on me, like I was a parcel.
My brother thought it was silly and took his off.
We left on a cold morning, and there was lots of steam.
The seats were green, and there was a shelf above them for bags.
A man came and checked our tickets, and he smiled at me.
I looked out the window and counted all the things going by.
After that town there were fields, and the cows were lying down.
He read his book and pretended he was not excited.
A woman got on with a basket and a bird that made noise.
She gave us some sweets and told us all about her family.
Then we went up high, and everything outside went a dull colour.
There were animals on the track, and the man made the train shout.
I remember the smell of the flowers coming in through the window.
My brother put his book away and said it was a lovely view.
I was so surprised that he agreed with me.
The track went along the water, and there were big birds standing in it.
Then we went through a dark place and came out into the light.
I had never seen the sea before, and it looked like a big flat thing.
We got there in the afternoon, and my legs were stiff.
She was waiting there for us in her coat and her hat.
She hugged us so hard that my label fell off.
We carried our bags up a lot of steps because she wanted us to.
Her house smelled of fish and polish, and the bed had a nice cover.
That night I heard the noise from the sea and felt far from home.
In the morning we had fish for breakfast, and I did not like it.
We spent the week on the beach, looking for things and getting wet.
He found a big stone with a pattern and carried it everywhere.
She bought us each a sweet thing that had writing inside it.
Coming home, I cried at the station because I did not want to leave.
He pretended he had something in his eye, so I knew he felt the same.
The way back was quiet, and I fell asleep on him.
When we got home, Dad was there waiting for us in his work clothes.
He picked me up and spun me round, and I told him about the sea.
He said he knew because he could smell it on me.
Whenever I go anywhere now, I think about that little trip.
It showed me that going away is a good way to see what you love.

sentences: The celebration I remember best is the street party for the Jubilee in nineteen seventy-seven.
We were living on Ash Grove in Headingley then, in a house with a bay window.
Helen was two, and she wore a red paper crown that kept slipping over her eyes.
Weeks beforehand, Missus Garside from number nine formed a committee and appointed herself chairman.
She called a meeting in her front room and served sherry in egg cups.
Everyone was given a job, and mine was to organise the cakes.
Alan was asked to draw a plan of the tables because he was the draughtsman.
He spent three evenings with a ruler and a set square and produced something worthy of a cathedral.
The tables came from the church hall and the school, and none of them matched.
We covered them with bedsheets and fastened the corners with clothes pegs.
Bunting went up on the Saturday, hundreds of little red, white and blue flags strung between the lamp posts.
Mister Gill from the corner shop lent us a ladder and held it, rather nervously.
The forecast was dreadful, but on the morning itself the sun came out.
By noon the whole street was carrying plates, jugs and folding chairs into the road.
There were sausage rolls, egg sandwiches, trifles in glass bowls and a jelly shaped like a rabbit.
I made forty fairy cakes and iced them in red and blue with a silver ball on each.
Old Mister Ackroyd from number four sat at the head of the table in his medals and an overcoat.
He said he had been to three coronations and a hundred funerals, and he preferred parties.
The children ran races in the road, and Missus Garside blew a whistle like a referee.
The egg and spoon race was won by a boy who had cheated, and nobody minded.
Then came the tug of war, the men against the women, and we won.
Alan fell flat on his back in the gutter, and the whole street cheered.
A man from the pub brought a piano on a cart, and we sang until our throats hurt.
I remember Missus Garside conducting with a wooden spoon during the hymns.
In mid afternoon the clouds rolled in, and big warm drops of rain began to fall.
Nobody went home, because the food was still on the tables and the singing was too good.
We dragged the tables together under the railway bridge at the end of the street.
The bridge echoed, and our singing sounded like a cathedral choir.
Helen fell asleep on a pile of coats with jelly on her chin.
As evening came, someone lit a fire in an old oil drum, and we toasted marshmallows.
The teenagers danced to a record player on a very long cable from Missus Garside's window.
Alan danced with me, and he was terrible, as always, but he held on tightly.
I remember the smell of wet pavement, woodsmoke and cold tea.
By eleven the children were asleep on laps, and the grown-ups were quiet.
We stacked the chairs and washed the cups in a bowl on the pavement.
Mister Ackroyd shook my hand and said it was the finest day since the war ended.
The next morning the street looked tired, with soggy bunting and one lonely shoe in the road.
We found a hundred pennies in the gutter, which had fallen from someone's pockets.
Missus Garside collected them and gave them to the hospital in the name of the street.
That was the first time I realised how a street can become a family.
We stayed in that house for twenty years, and we never had another party like it.
Whenever I see bunting now, I can smell the rain and hear that piano.
vague_sentences: The party I remember best was the one we had in the street.
We lived in a house there, and it had a big window.
Our little girl wore a paper hat that kept falling over her eyes.
Before that, a woman from down the road started a group and took charge.
She had a meeting at her house and gave everyone some drink.
Everyone got a job, and mine was to do the food.
My husband had to draw a plan of the tables.
He worked on it for days, and it looked very grand.
The tables came from places nearby, and none of them looked alike.
We put sheets on them and held the corners down with little things.
On Saturday we put up lots of little flags between the posts.
A man from the shop lent us a ladder and held it.
They said it would be a bad day, but the sun came out.
By midday everyone was carrying their things out into the road.
There was lots of food, and some of it was shaped like animals.
I made a lot of little cakes and put something shiny on top.
An old man sat at the front with his coat on.
He said he had been to lots of things like this, and he liked parties best.
The children ran races, and the woman blew a whistle for them.
A boy won one race by cheating, and nobody cared.
Then there was a pulling game, and we won.
My husband fell down in the road, and everyone cheered.
Someone brought an instrument on a cart, and we sang until we were hoarse.
I remember that woman waving a stick at us while we sang.
Later the sky went dark, and it started to rain on us.
Nobody went home, because the food was out and everyone was having fun.
We pushed it all together under the thing at the end of the road.
It made a lot of noise, and the singing sounded wonderful in there.
Our little girl fell asleep on some coats with food on her face.
When it got dark, someone made a fire, and we cooked sweet things on it.
The young ones danced to music from a window with a very long wire.
My husband danced with me, and he was bad at it, but held me tight.
I remember the smell of the wet road and the smoke.
By late evening all the children were asleep, and the rest of us were quiet.
We put the chairs away and washed the cups in a bowl.
The old man shook my hand and said it was the best day for years.
The next morning the street looked tired, with wet flags and a shoe lying there.
We found lots of coins in the gutter that had fallen out of people's pockets.
The woman took them and gave them to the place where I worked.
That was when I saw that a street can feel like a family.
We stayed in that house a long time, and we never had another day like it.
When I see little flags now, I can smell the rain and hear that music.

sentences: The meal that brings everything back is my mother's Sunday dinner on Hollin Road.
It always began on Saturday night, when she scrubbed the potatoes and peeled the carrots.
On Sunday morning she rose early and lit the range.
The joint was usually a piece of brisket or a small leg of lamb from Mister Hartley the butcher.
If money was short, it was a boiled bacon knuckle with parsley sauce.
She rubbed the meat with dripping and salt and slid it into the oven.
Then she made the batter for the Yorkshire puddings, and this was serious business.
She used plain flour, eggs, milk and a pinch of salt, and she let it rest in the pantry.
She believed the secret was a smoking hot tin and a quick pour, and she never wrote it down.
When the tin came out, the fat spat and sizzled, and we all stood back.
She poured the batter in with one swift movement, and it rose like little golden hats.
We ate the Yorkshire pudding first, on its own, with thick onion gravy.
My father said it filled you up so you needed less meat, which was the point.
Then came the roast, the potatoes crisp at the edges, and cabbage boiled until it gave up.
There were carrots cut into coins and mint sauce from mint that grew by the yard wall.
Peter always took the crispiest potato, and I always complained, and my mother always ignored us both.
Nobody spoke much during the meal, because everyone was busy and the food was hot.
Afterwards there was rhubarb crumble, or a suet pudding with golden syrup poured on top.
The rhubarb came from my grandmother's allotment in Armley, pink and sharp.
My mother sprinkled sugar on it and baked it until the top turned the colour of sand.
With custard, it was the nearest thing to heaven I knew as a child.
After dinner my father fell asleep in his chair with a newspaper over his face.
Peter and I dried the dishes while my mother washed and told us stories.
The leftovers became bubble and squeak on Monday, fried in a black pan until crusty.
Nothing was wasted in that house, and I think that is why everything tasted so good.
When I left home to train, I missed those dinners more than I missed anything else.
In the nurses' home we ate grey mince, and I felt thoroughly sorry for myself.
Whenever I came home on a Sunday, my mother put an extra potato on my plate without comment.
After I married, I tried to make her Yorkshire puddings, and the first batch was as flat as pennies.
I rang her up in tears, and she laughed and told me the tin had not been hot enough.
It took me a year to get it right, and Alan ate every failure with a brave face.
When Helen was little, she called them the puffy ones and would eat nothing else.
Now I make them every Sunday in Abu Dhabi for Helen and the children.
The oven is gas and shiny and far too modern, but the batter is my mother's.
Ruby counts the minutes at the oven door with her nose almost touching the glass.
Sam says they are the only English food he likes, and I take that as a compliment.
I buy the flour from a little shop near the Corniche, and the shopkeeper knows me by name.
When the puddings rise, I feel that my mother is standing right beside me in the kitchen.
She would have scolded me for the heat in this country and for the thin cabbage.
But she would have eaten two helpings, and she would have asked for the recipe.
vague_sentences: The meal that brings it all back is the one my mum made on Sundays.
It always started the night before, when she got everything ready.
On Sunday she got up early and lit the fire before Dad came home.
The meat was usually something from the man at the shop.
If there was not much money, it was something cheaper with a sauce.
She put some fat on it and put it in the oven.
Then she made the mixture for the puddings, and that was a serious job.
She used the usual things and left it to sit in the cold.
She said the secret was a hot tin, and she never wrote it down.
When the tin came out, the fat was noisy and we stood back.
She poured it in fast, and soon they had risen up all golden.
We ate those first, on their own, with lots of gravy.
Dad said it filled you up so you did not need so much meat.
Then came the meat, the potatoes, and the green stuff cooked for ages.
There were carrots in little bits and some sauce from the plant by the wall.
My brother always took the best potato, and I always moaned, and Mum ignored us.
Nobody said much while we ate, because it was hot and we were busy.
After that there was something sweet, with sauce poured on top.
The sweet stuff came from my gran's place, pink and a bit sour.
Mum put sugar on it and cooked it until the top went brown.
With the yellow sauce, it was the nicest thing I knew as a child.
After the meal Dad fell asleep in his chair with the paper on his face.
We dried the dishes while she washed, and she told us stories.
The leftover food got fried up on Monday in a black pan.
Nothing was thrown away there, and I think that is why it was good.
When I left home, I missed those meals more than anything else.
Where I lived then, the food was grey and horrible, and I felt sorry for myself.
Whenever I went home on a Sunday, Mum gave me extra without saying anything.
After I got married, I tried to make hers, and the first lot came out flat.
I rang her up crying, and she laughed and said the tin was not hot enough.
It took me ages to get it right, and he ate the bad ones.
When our girl was little, she called them the puffy ones and ate nothing else.
Now I make them every Sunday for her and the little ones.
The oven here is new and shiny, but the mixture is the same as Mum's.
The little girl stands at the oven door with her nose on the glass.
The boy says it is the only English food he likes, and I take that well.
I get the stuff from a little shop near the sea, and the man knows me.
When they rise, I feel like Mum is standing right there next to me.
She would have grumbled about the heat here and the thin green stuff.
But she would have had two helpings and asked how I made them.

sentences: The biggest move of my life came in the spring of two thousand and seventeen.
Alan had been gone for two years, and the house in Headingley had grown far too quiet.
Helen rang me every Sunday from Abu Dhabi, and every Sunday she asked the same question.
She asked if I might come and live near her and the children.
I said no for a long time, because I was a Yorkshire woman and Yorkshire women stay put.
Then one February morning I slipped on the ice outside the front door, and that decided it.
I was not hurt, but I lay there looking at the sky and thought how silly it was.
I called Helen from the kitchen floor and told her I would come.
Selling the house took three months, and I cried over every cupboard.
I found Alan's pencil tin, his rolled drawings in the attic, and a dried rose from our wedding.
I gave his drawing board to a young architect from down the road, and it felt right.
My brother Peter drove over from Harrogate with a van and helped me sort what to keep.
We argued over the barometer, which was our father's, and in the end Peter kept it.
I took my sewing box, my good knives and a suitcase of photographs.
The rest went to charity shops, and I watched the van pull away with a lump in my throat.
On the last night I slept on a camp bed in the empty front room.
Next morning the taxi took me to the airport, and Doreen waved from her gate.
I had never liked flying, so I held a mint tight and looked at the seat in front.
We landed in Abu Dhabi at night, and the warm air hit me like an opened oven door.
Helen was waiting in arrivals with Sam on her shoulders and Ruby holding a paper sign.
The sign said welcome Grandma, and the letters were all different colours.
My new flat was in Khalidiyah, on the ninth floor, with a balcony facing the sea.
For the first week I could not sleep, because the sun was so bright and the quiet so strange.
The heat was the hardest part, and I walked to the shop only at dawn.
Everything smelled different, of cardamom and diesel and the sea, and no rain fell for months.
I missed the green terribly, and I stood on the balcony wishing for one muddy field.
So I bought pots and compost and planted mint, basil and a stubborn little rosemary.
The rosemary died twice, and the third one is still alive, and I am very proud of it.
Helen took me to the souk, and I learned to haggle with a straight face.
A woman in the building named Fatima brought me dates and cardamom coffee on my second day.
We could hardly understand each other, but we sat together and laughed at the same things.
Within a month I had found a choir in a church hall near the harbour.
We were Filipino, Indian, Irish and Egyptian, and we sang Handel with the air conditioning on full.
I felt like a seedling that had been moved into a bigger pot.
Ruby came on Thursdays to bake with me, and Sam came to show me his school projects.
Some nights I still feel very far from Leeds, especially when I remember the rain.
I ring Peter every Sunday, and he tells me about the weather in Yorkshire with great relish.
I do not regret the move, but I do not pretend it was easy.
Home turned out to be less about a place and more about who comes to dinner.
And my kitchen, with its Yorkshire tea and a little rosemary, is home enough.
vague_sentences: The biggest move in my life was a long time ago, in the spring.
My husband had gone by then, and the house felt far too quiet.
Our girl rang me every week, and every week she asked me the same thing.
She asked if I would come and live near her and the little ones.
I said no for a long time, because we stay put up north.
Then one morning I fell on the ice outside, and that made me decide.
I was not hurt, but I lay there looking up and thought it was silly.
I rang her from the floor and told her I would come.
Selling the house took ages, and I cried over every cupboard.
I found his things in a tin, and a dry flower from the wedding.
I gave his old table to a young man, and that felt right.
My brother came in a van and helped me sort out what to keep.
We argued over a thing that was our dad's, and he took it in the end.
I took my sewing things, some good bits from the kitchen, and a case of photos.
The rest went to the shops, and I watched the van go sadly.
On the last night I slept on a little bed in the empty room.
In the morning a car took me to the airport, and someone waved.
I never liked flying, so I held a sweet and looked straight ahead.
We got there at night, and the warm air hit me like a hot oven.
My girl was waiting there with the little ones and a sign.
The sign said hello to me, in all different colours.
My new flat was high up, and it had a little balcony looking at the sea.
For a week I could not sleep, because it was so bright and so quiet.
The heat was the worst thing, and I only went out at dawn.
Everything smelled different, and it did not rain for ages.
I missed the green so much and stood outside wishing for a muddy field.
So I bought pots and soil and planted some herbs, and one stubborn little plant.
That plant died twice, and the third is still going, and I am proud.
My girl took me to the market, and I learned to bargain.
A woman in the building brought me sweet things and a hot drink.
We hardly understood each other, but we sat together and laughed at the same things.
Within a month I found a group who sang, in a room near the water.
They were from all sorts of places, and we sang old songs.
I felt like a little plant that had been moved into a bigger pot.
The little girl came to cook with me, and the boy showed me his work.
Some nights I still feel very far from home, especially when it rains.
I ring my brother every Sunday, and he tells me all about the weather there.
I do not regret it, but I do not say it was easy.
Home turned out to be about the people, more than the place.
And my kitchen, with the tea and the little plant, is home enough.

sentences: A typical day as a ward sister began at five in the morning, in the dark.
I lived in Headingley then and caught the first bus, the number twelve, with the milkmen.
I arrived at Saint Aldric's by six, and the night staff were grey with tiredness.
We sat in the ward kitchen with strong tea and a plate of toast for the handover.
The night sister read out each patient from a battered notebook, bed by bed.
I wrote everything on a slip of paper and tucked it into my apron pocket.
By half past six the ward lights went on, and the day truly began.
The ward was long, with twenty-eight beds and tall windows down both sides.
The floor was polished lino, and you could hear a pair of shoes coming from the far door.
First came the bedpans and washing, with bowls of warm water carried on trays.
Every bed was stripped and made with hospital corners, and I checked each one with my hand.
A crooked sheet meant a crooked day, as far as I was concerned.
Breakfast arrived on a trolley with big steel urns of tea, porridge and bread and margarine.
The patients who could sit up ate at a table, and I always sat with the grumpy ones.
After breakfast came the medicine round, with the drug trolley and its jangling keys.
I counted tablets into tiny glass cups, and two nurses had to sign for anything dangerous.
At nine the doctors came in a cluster, with the consultant at the front like a ship's captain.
I walked beside him with the charts and told him honestly what the night had been like.
Mid morning was dressings and drips, and the sterilised instruments came in a steel drum.
I used a tray of forceps, gauze and iodine, and my hands never shook.
At eleven the tea trolley rattled in, and the whole ward breathed out together.
Dinner at noon was minced beef, mashed potato and boiled swede.
I tasted it myself each day, because a sister who has not tasted it cannot complain.
Visiting began at two, and the relatives arrived with flowers, grapes and nervous faces.
I stood at the ward door and spoke to each family, because nobody should walk in without a word.
Afternoons brought the students, and I taught them to take a pulse with a watch with a second hand.
I told them that a pulse is a conversation, and they should listen to it properly.
At three there was always a crisis of some kind, a fall or a faint or a blocked drip.
We dealt with it, and nobody outside ever knew how close it had been.
Matron Fairweather came round at four in her starched cap, and every nurse stood straighter.
She ran a finger along the window sills and looked at it, and she nearly always said nothing.
At six the evening staff arrived, and I handed over, bed by bed, from my own slip of paper.
Before leaving I walked the ward once more, saying goodnight to every patient by name.
Mister Jenkins in bed fourteen always held up two fingers, meaning he was alive and cross.
I went home on the bus with sore feet and a head full of names.
Alan had the dinner on the table, usually cheese on toast, and I thought it the finest meal in Leeds.
Helen would be doing her homework at the kitchen table with her tongue between her teeth.
I put my feet in a bowl of salt water and read the paper for ten minutes.
Then I slept like a stone and woke at five to begin again.
It was hard and tiring work, but I would not swap one hour of it.
vague_sentences: A normal day at work started very early, while it was still dark.
I lived a long way off then and took the first bus with the milk men.
I got there at six, and the people from the night were tired.
We sat in the little kitchen with tea and toast while they told us things.
The woman in charge read out every person from a worn notebook.
I wrote it all on a bit of paper and put it in my pocket.
By half past six the lights were on, and the day began.
It was a big long room with lots of beds and tall windows.
The floor was shiny, and you could hear anyone walking from the far end.
First came the washing, with bowls of warm water on trays.
Every bed was stripped and done again properly, and I checked each one.
A bad bed meant a bad day, as far as I was concerned.
Food came on a trolley with big tins of tea and porridge and bread.
Those who could sit up ate at a table, and I sat with the grumpy ones.
After that there was the round with the trolley and the keys that jangled.
I counted the tablets into little cups, and two of us had to sign.
At nine the doctors came in a group, with the important one at the front.
I walked next to him with the papers and told him how the night had been.
Later in the morning there were wounds to do and things to put up on poles.
I used a tray of tools and bandages, and my hands never shook.
At eleven the tea came, and the whole room seemed to relax.
At midday the food was meat and mash and something orange, then pudding with sauce.
I tried it myself every day, because you cannot complain if you have not tried it.
After lunch the visitors came with flowers and fruit and worried faces.
I stood at the door and spoke to each family, because nobody should go in alone.
In the afternoon the young ones came, and I showed them things.
I told them that it was like talking, and they should listen.
At three something always went wrong, like a fall or a faint or a blocked thing.
We dealt with it, and nobody outside ever knew how close it was.
The big boss came round at four in her stiff hat, and everyone stood up straight.
She ran a finger along the window and looked at it, and said nothing.
At six the next people came, and I told them about everyone from my paper.
Before I left, I walked round again and said goodnight to each person.
One man in the end bed held up two fingers, meaning he was alive and cross.
I went home on the bus with sore feet and my head full of names.
My husband had made something for dinner, nothing special, but I thought it was lovely.
Our girl would be doing her work at the table with her tongue out.
I put my feet in a bowl and read the paper for a bit.
Then I slept like a stone and got up early to do it all again.
It was hard work and tiring, but I would not change a minute of it.

sentences: The thing I am proudest of is the garden we built at Saint Aldric's in nineteen ninety-four.
I was ward sister on the old people's ward by then, on the second floor.
Our patients stared all day at a brick wall, and I hated it.
Below the ward was a little courtyard full of broken pallets, rusty bedframes and nettles.
One morning I looked down from the window and decided it would be a garden.
I wrote a letter to the hospital board, and it came back with a polite refusal.
I wrote another, and the board sent me a note about budgets and insurance.
So I stopped writing letters and started digging instead, early on Sunday mornings.
Alan came with his spade and a flask of tea, and he said I was mad, but he came.
We cleared the nettles first, and I will never forget how they stung through my gloves.
A porter called Dennis dragged the rusty bedframes away on a trolley and asked no questions.
The maintenance man, Mister Pritchard, found us some old paving slabs from a demolished wing.
I wrote to every garden centre in West Yorkshire asking for odds and ends.
A nursery in Otley sent us forty rose bushes and a barrow of compost for nothing.
The choir I sang in at the time held a cake sale and raised enough for a bench.
We built raised beds at wheelchair height, so that nobody had to bend down to touch a plant.
I planted lavender along the path, because the smell is calming and the bees love it.
The sweet peas went up a trellis that Alan made from bean poles and garden twine.
Some of the older nurses thought I had lost my mind, and one said it was not nursing.
I told her that I believed it was exactly what nursing was.
The first patient to go out was Missus Brearley, who had not spoken for a month.
Two nurses wheeled her down, and she looked at the lavender and put her hand in it.
She said it smelled like her mother's linen cupboard, and then she cried quietly.
After that the ward changed, and I could feel it, like a window opened in a stuffy room.
Men who had refused to get out of bed asked for a cushion and a cardigan.
We held a tea party in July, with scones and a small brass band from the colliery.
Even the consultant came down, and he ate three scones and admitted I had been right.
The board came to inspect, and I stood by the roses with my heart in my throat.
The chairman looked at the patients laughing in the sun and took off his hat.
He said that perhaps the wall should have been a garden all along.
They gave us a small budget the next year, and I spent every penny on bulbs.
Spring after spring the daffodils came up, and the patients held them like small trumpets.
When I retired in two thousand and seven, the staff named a bench after me.
It had a small brass plate, and I felt too shy to read it out loud.
I have never been much good at speeches, and I was not asked to make one.
Instead, the nurses sang for me, rather badly, and I loved every note.
I am proud of Helen's buildings and of Sam's drawings, but that garden was my own.
It showed me that a stubborn woman with a spade can change a whole ward.
I have heard that it is still there, though the old wing has been rebuilt around it.
Whenever I smell lavender, I think of that tiny square of earth and of Missus Brearley's hand.
vague_sentences: The thing I am proudest of is the garden we made at work.
I was in charge of the older people's part, up on the second floor.
The people there looked at a wall all day, and I hated that.
Down below was a little place full of old rusty things and weeds.
One morning I looked down from the window and decided it should be a garden.
I wrote to the people in charge, and they said no, politely.
I wrote again, and they sent me a note about money and rules.
So I stopped writing and started digging, early on Sundays.
My husband came with a spade, and he said I was mad, but he came.
We did the weeds first, and they stung me right through my gloves.
A man took the rusty things away on a trolley and asked nothing.
Another man found us some old stones from a building that had come down.
I wrote to lots of places asking for anything they could spare.
One place sent us a load of plants and some soil for nothing.
The group I sang with did a sale and made enough for a seat.
We made beds that were up high, so nobody had to bend down to touch things.
I put some purple plants along the path, because they smell nice and bees like them.
The flowers went up a frame that my husband made from sticks and string.
Some of the older staff thought I was mad, and one said it was not work.
I told her I thought it was exactly what the work was.
The first person to go out was a woman who had not spoken for ages.
Two of them took her down, and she put her hand in the plants.
She said it smelled like her mum's cupboard, and then she cried quietly.
After that, the whole place changed, like a window opened in a stuffy room.
Men who would not get out of bed asked for a blanket and a coat.
We had a tea party in the summer, with cakes and some men with instruments.
Even the important man came, and he ate lots and said I was right.
The people in charge came to look, and I stood there feeling very nervous.
The big man looked at everyone laughing in the sun and took off his hat.
He said maybe that wall should have been a garden all along.
They gave us some money the next year, and I spent every bit on flowers.
Every spring they came up, and the old people held them like little horns.
When I stopped working, the staff put my name on a seat.
It had a little plate, and I felt too shy to read it out.
I was never good at speeches, and nobody asked me to make one.
Instead they sang for me, rather badly, and I loved it.
I am proud of what they make, but that garden was mine.
It showed me that one stubborn person with a spade can change a place.
I heard it is still there, even though they built around it.
When I smell those purple flowers, I think of that place and that woman's hand.

anecdote_retellings: When I first started nursing, there was an old man in the ward who worked with wood.
He made me a little bird for my birthday.
It was a tiny thing, no bigger than my thumb.
I put it on my windowsill at home, and it is still there.
A man who used to make furniture was ill in my ward one winter.
He gave me a present that he had made himself, a small bird.
I think he did it because it was a special day for me.
Now it sits in my kitchen by the window.
I had a patient once who was very kind to me.
He was good with his hands, and he made me something for my birthday.
It was a little bird, and he gave it to me with a smile.
I look at it every morning when I make my tea.
It always reminds me of him.
